5.In FLINTKOTE COMPANY v. ACIA PLC, 177 F.Supp.3d 1165, 1174 (N.D.Cal. 2016), an insurance contract’s choice-of-law provision
stated that disputes were to be resolved “in accordance with applicable common law of the states of the United States.” The district court rejected the
argument that this provision allowed it to rely on “generally applicable contract interpretation rules that apply to insurance policies,” because that
would be inconsistent with Erie’s guidance that “there is no such thing as a ‘national common law.’ ” Instead, the court looked to Klaxon and the
presumption that in a diversity case, the court will look first to the conflicts principles of the forum state. Under that test, the California choice-of-law
rule applied, which required the application of California substantive law. Was this decision analytically sound? Was it wise?
2.ASCERTAINING THE STATE LAW
MASON V. AMERICAN EMERY WHEEL WORKS
United States Court of Appeals, First Circuit, 1957.
241 F.2d 906.
MAGRUDER, CHIEF JUDGE. Whit Mason, a citizen of Mississippi, filed his complaint in the United States District Court for the District of
Rhode Island against The American Emery Wheel Works, a Rhode Island corporation. The case was one in tort for personal injuries
alleged to have been suffered by the plaintiff in Mississippi as a result of negligent misfeasance by the defendant in putting out in
commerce without adequate care and inspection, a dangerously defective emery wheel. According to the allegations of the complaint, at
some time prior to the date of the accident defendant negligently manufactured, inspected and tested a certain emery wheel designed for
attachment to a bench grinder; that due to such negligence the emery wheel was not reasonably fit for the use for which it was intended,
but on the contrary subjected to a risk of personal injury all persons lawfully using a bench grinder with the emery wheel attached * * *.
* * *
